source.title: Four nucleon systems: a zoom to the open problems in nuclear interaction

accepted.question_text: How can few-nucleon nuclear interaction models be constrained so that one can determine whether missing physics in systems with more than two nucleons should be represented as explicit three-nucleon forces or instead absorbed into nonlocal two-nucleon off-shell terms? Binding energies of light nuclei alone are insufficient because low-energy few-nucleon binding depends on very few parameters and can be fitted by adding three-nucleon forces or by changing nonlocal two-body interactions; the needed constraints should come from continuum observables, such as four-nucleon thresholds and resonances, that test different spatial configurations.
accepted.context_brief: Three-nucleon forces versus nonlocal two-nucleon off-shell effects

evidence.quote: A standard practice to account for the missing off-shell physics in description of N>2 nuclei is implementation of 3N forces. In such a manner it is not difficult to improve description of 3N and 4N binding energies. However such procedure, which relies only on good description of binding energies can be quite misleading.
Thus study of nuclear binding energies, even being of fundamental importance, can provide only very limited information on nuclear interaction structure.

One thus could expect that a substantial part of 3- and multi-nucleon forces could also be absorbed by nonlocal terms. A considerable simplification would result if the bulk of experimental data could be described by only using two-body nonlocal interaction.
Only careful analysis of continuum spectra, which enables one to test various space configurations, can impose stronger constrains to the off-shell structure of the nuclear interaction.

accepted.question_text: How should nonlocal INOY or Doleschall two-nucleon interaction models be modified so that they retain their ability to reproduce two-nucleon observables and overcome the missing three-nucleon binding energy without explicit three-nucleon forces, while also reproducing the alpha-particle binding energy and proton root-mean-square radius? The concrete failure mode is that these nonlocal models overbind the alpha particle by about 800 keV and predict a proton root-mean-square radius about 10% smaller than experiment, suggesting that the interactions are too soft and may need increased short-range repulsion between nucleons.

evidence.quote: They have managed to construct purely phenomenological nonlocal NN forces (called INOY), which are able to overcome the lack of binding energy in three-nucleon systems, without explicitly using 3NF and still reproducing 2N observables.

In contrary to 3N system, experimental value of α-particle binding energy is overestimated by ∼ 800 keV. Nevertheless this discrepancy is considerably smaller than for conventional local interaction models and is on a par with the result obtained using CD-Bonn NN in conjunction with Tucson-Melbourne 3NF.
In Table 1 one can clearly see that proton r.m.s. radius in α-particle predicted by INOY models is by ∼ 10% smaller than the experimental one.

Such tendency demonstrates that INOY interactions are too soft, resulting into a faster condensation of the nuclear matter. In order to improve these models one should try to increase the short range repulsion between the nucleons.

accepted.question_text: How can a nuclear interaction model simultaneously reproduce the alpha-particle ground state, the triton threshold, and the position and width of the first excited helium-4 state with spin-parity 0+ that controls very-low-energy proton plus tritium scattering below the neutron plus helium-3 threshold? The model must treat the Coulomb separation of the proton plus tritium and neutron plus helium-3 thresholds properly, because the low-energy excitation function and singlet scattering length are highly sensitive to whether the 0+ resonance is placed correctly relative to those thresholds.
accepted.context_brief: Placement of the first excited helium-4 0+ resonance

evidence.quote: Separation of n+3He and p+3H channels requires proper treatment of Coulomb interaction, the task is furthermore burden since both thresholds are described by the same isospin quantum numbers.

In order to reproduce the shape of experimental excitation function, NN interaction model is obliged with high accurately situate 4He excited state. In fact, width of the resonance is strongly correlated with its relative position to p+3H threshold.

As have been shown, description of low energy p+3H completely relies on success in reproducing position and width of the first excited state of α-particle. However position of this resonant state seems to be strongly correlated with position of predicted triton threshold and α-particle ground state.

accepted.question_text: What interaction effects are still missing in low-energy neutron plus tritium scattering when a model such as AV18 plus Urbana IX three-nucleon force already reproduces the triton binding energy, yet the coherent scattering lengths remain less clearly consistent with experiment? The question concerns the zero-energy and very-low-energy neutron plus tritium observables, where the zero-energy cross section may fit experimental data while coherent scattering lengths still show small discrepancies.

evidence.quote: However even implementing UIX 3NF for AV18 model, and thus reproducing triton binding energy, small discrepancies remain [11]. If zero energy cross section seems to fit experimental data, agreement for the coherent scattering lengths is less obvious.
Nonlocal interaction model (INOY04) reproduces low n+3H energy data better, this fact is best reflected near the elastic cross section minima around Ecm ∼ 0.4 MeV, see Fig. 2.

accepted.question_text: What missing nuclear-interaction physics causes realistic interaction models, including INOY and AV18 plus Urbana IX, to underestimate neutron plus tritium elastic cross sections by more than 10% in the resonance region near center-of-mass energy about 3 MeV? This problem is not resolved by the same off-shell effects, explicit three-nucleon forces, or nonlocal two-nucleon forces that improve lower-energy behavior, so the cause must be sought in interaction components that affect the negative-parity resonance region.

evidence.quote: Nevertheless this system contains two, spin degenerated, narrow resonances at low energy (Ecm ≈ 3 MeV), while ability of nuclear interaction models to describe scattering cross sections in this resonance region was put in doubt [15, 16].

Nevertheless all realistic interaction models, including INOY, underestimate by more than 10% elastic cross sections in the resonance region. Off-shell effects as 3NF or nonlocality of the force, which improve low energy behavior, do not give sizeable effect.
On the other hand contribution of NN P-wave becomes almost as important as one of S-waves in negative parity states for n+3H resonance region.

accepted.question_text: Are nucleon-nucleon P-wave interactions, especially neutron-neutron P-waves and their charge dependence, incorrectly constrained in current nuclear interaction models, and can a physically acceptable P-wave correction explain the neutron plus tritium resonance-region disagreement and related failures in neutron-rich or P-wave-sensitive observables? The motivation is that neutron-neutron P-waves are not directly controlled by experiment, that a roughly 20% change in the neutron-neutron P-wave potential would be needed for AV18 to describe the resonance cross sections, and that discrepancies in helium-isotope binding energies grow with neutron excess even when three-nucleon forces improve the overall agreement.

evidence.quote: On contrary rare physical observables, where NN P-waves are important, have tendency to disagree with the experimental data. One such example could be the 3N analyzing powers [17, 18]. Higher NN waves should contribute in asymmetric nuclear systems; n+3H system due to its large neutron excess is one such case.
The discrepancy increases linearly with neutron excess, even if 3NF improves overall agreement it does not remove this tendency.

All these statements speaks against good description of NN interaction in P-waves. One should also recall that NN interaction is basically tuned on n-p and p-p data. Moreover, low energy p-p P-waves are overcasted by Coulomb repulsion, while n-n P-waves are not directly controlled by experiment at all.

We have evaluated, see Fig. 3, how much n-n P-wave potential must be changed in order to describe resonance cross sections for Av18 model. It turns to be of order ∼ 20%, which is rather much to blame on charge dependence in P-waves as well as compared to ∼ 6-8% necessary to solve Ay puzzle in n-d scattering [17, 18].
Still this study suggests that charge dependence effects can be sizeable in n-n P-waves and can provide a possible explanation for the disagreement observed in n-3H resonance region.

trace.notes: Resolved arXiv abs URL to the PDF and mapped the paper into title/abstract, introduction, theoretical model, alpha-particle, p+3H scattering, n+3H elastic scattering, acknowledgments, and references. Likely open-problem regions were concentrated in the introduction, alpha-particle discussion, p+3H low-energy resonance discussion, and n+3H resonance/P-wave discussion.

Extracted an implicit question about how to constrain missing off-shell physics and the division between explicit 3NF and nonlocal NN terms, because the text says binding-energy fits can be misleading and limited.

Extracted an implicit question about improving INOY/Doleschall nonlocal interactions because the text reports successful 3N binding without explicit 3NF but alpha-particle overbinding and too-small radius.

Extracted an implicit question about correctly placing the first excited helium-4 0+ state and treating Coulomb-separated p+3H and n+3He thresholds because the excitation function is resonance-sensitive.
Extracted an implicit question about residual low-energy n+3H discrepancies after fixing triton binding, specifically coherent scattering lengths.
Extracted implicit questions about the n+3H resonance-region cross-section deficit and the possible role of NN P-waves, especially n-n P-waves and charge dependence.

Expanded the compact source discussion into a self-contained question defining the decision between explicit three-nucleon forces and nonlocal two-nucleon off-shell terms, and included the source's continuum-observable constraint requirement.
Expanded INOY/Doleschall model deficiencies into a standalone model-improvement question and included the overbinding, radius, softness, and short-range-repulsion evidence.
Expanded the p+3H resonance discussion into a standalone question that states the relevant channels, threshold separation, and dependence on the first excited helium-4 0+ state.
Expanded the residual n+3H low-energy discrepancy into a question about missing interaction effects after triton binding is reproduced.

Expanded the resonance-region cross-section underprediction into a standalone question and explicitly excluded 3NF/nonlocality as sufficient explanations because the source says they do not give sizeable effects there.

Expanded the P-wave and charge-dependence discussion into a standalone question about whether n-n P-waves are incorrectly constrained and whether a physically acceptable correction can explain neutron-rich and resonance discrepancies.

Kept six accepted questions. The n+3H resonance deficit and the n-n P-wave/charge-dependence hypothesis are related but distinct: one asks what missing physics causes the failed observable, while the other asks whether a specific candidate mechanism is viable and constrained.
All accepted questions passed self-containedness, evidence coverage, evidence completeness, no-new-facts, source adequacy, and schema conformance gates. No candidates were moved to needs_review.
